rappel_detail.notes: First of two double-rope (60m) rappels; some downclimbing needed to reach the next station.
rappel_detail.anchor: trees/rock horn near head of gully

rappel_detail.notes: Second double-rope rappel reaching easier snow near the gully's base.

wa_chair_peak_north_face.rappels: Typically a single 60m rappel (occasionally two) through the summit gully/notch back into the basin; some late-day/crowded ascents have required additional downclimbing when rope length fell short
wa_chair_peak_north_face.rappel_count_note: The two counts on this page are the same descent with a different rope setup, not a disagreement. The gully on the south side of the east face goes in one 60 m double-rope rappel, or in the two ~30 m single-rope rappels listed here. How much you rappel at all depends on conditions: with good steep snow much of it is downclimbed, and parties describe reaching the base on a single rappel plus downclimbing. Two rappel stations were added in early summer 2023 so that a 60 m rope makes every rappel on the route - several leave under 5 ft of rope spare, so knot the ends.
wa_chair_peak_north_face.descent_text: From the summit, most parties reverse toward the notch/col below the summit block and descend the gully on the south side of the east face (sometimes described as the same gully used by the Northeast Buttress descent). Expect a mix of downclimbing and rappelling: parties commonly do two double-rope (60m) rappels — the first from trees/rock anchors near the head of the gully with some downclimbing to reach the next station, and a second double-rope rappel that reaches easier snow near the gully's base — though some parties describe reaching the base with a single 60m rappel plus downclimbing depending on snow coverage. Anchors are a mix of natural gear (trees, rock horns/slings) rather than bolts; bring cord/webbing to back up or replace tattered slings. From the base of the gully, downclimb snow/talus east back into the Chair Peak basin and pick up the approach trail to Source Lake and out. Watch for cornices at the gully lip early season, loose rock in the gully when snow-free, and wet-slide hazard on the descent slopes during warm spring conditions.

wa_garfield_mountain_preiss_route.rappels: No fixed rappel line on the route. Descend over the main West Peak summit and down the west ridge, or - if you have carried two 60 m ropes - rappel Infinite Bliss instead: counts for this rappel line differ - about 20 to 25 double-rope rappels. Do not head straight down the northwest backside slope.
wa_garfield_mountain_preiss_route.descent_text: From the sub-summit, walk down and left through the small gap in the trees onto the gentle northern slope, then go up and over the main West Peak summit and descend the west ridge. Do NOT head straight down the northwest backside slope — the first ascensionist flags this specifically. The alternative, if you have carried two 60 m ropes, is to rappel Infinite Bliss (about 20 rappels off the chain stations); a single 70 m or 80 m is not long enough for those stations. Either way this is a long descent on brushy, disorienting terrain and should be started with hours of daylight in hand.

rappel_detail.notes: West Ridge rappel 1 of 5 on a single 60-70 m rope.
rappel_detail.anchor: fixed slings and rap rings, or a nut anchor built on the spot
hazards: Back up or replace any tattered tat: carry extra cord and a knife.
rappel_detail.station: Summit area, at the top of the West Ridge crest. The fixed stations here have been found both freshly rebuilt and badly tattered, so inspect each one.

rappel_detail.notes: West Ridge rappel 2 of 5 on a single 60-70 m rope.
rappel_detail.anchor: fixed slings and rap rings of varying quality, or natural nut and cam anchors
hazards: Some rappels traverse sideways to reach the next anchor. Loose, rockfall-prone rock sits on these traversing lines, so move one at a time and keep the rope out of the fall line.
rappel_detail.station: Next station down the upper West Ridge crest. Some stations sit off to the side rather than straight below the last, to keep you out of the fall line.

rappel_detail.notes: West Ridge rappel 5 of 5 on a single 60-70 m rope. Below it, coil the rope and downclimb 3rd-4th class terrain to the notch at the top of the South Face.
rappel_detail.anchor: fixed slings and rap rings of varying quality, or natural nut and cam anchors
rappel_detail.station: Next station down the upper West Ridge crest, the last one before the ridge eases. Some stations sit off to the side rather than straight below the last, to keep you out of the fall line.

rappel_detail.anchor: fixed slings and rap rings, or natural anchors
rappel_detail.station: The notch at the top of the South Face, reached by the downclimb from the last ridge station.

hazards: Several South Face rappels need a hard traverse one way or the other to reach the next anchor. Weight the rope before you swing, and watch for rock knocked loose by the rope.

rappel_detail.notes: South Face rappel 9 of 9. This one often takes the full length of the doubled rope to reach flat glacier snow; knot the ends. Rope up for glacier travel as soon as you are down.
rappel_detail.anchor: fixed slings and rap rings, or natural anchors
hazards: Crevasses on the Terror Glacier start right at the bottom of the rappel.
rappel_detail.station: Lowest station on the South Face, above the Terror Glacier.

wa_south_face_5.rappels: 14 single-rope rappels with a 60-70 m rope: 5 down the upper West Ridge, a scramble down to a notch, then 9 down the South Face to the Terror Glacier. With two ropes, parties have made seven double-rope rappels instead.
wa_south_face_5.rappel_count_note: Counted for one 60-70 m rope, which is what most parties now carry: 5 rappels on the upper West Ridge and 9 on the South Face below the notch. The stations are spaced for a single rope. With two ropes, parties have descended the whole West Ridge in seven double-rope rappels off natural anchors instead, skipping the South Face. Anchors on the ridge were reported rebuilt in June 2024, but stations vary and some are tattered, so carry cord to back them up. Two landmarks on the ridge part of the line: a large horn anchor, and a fixed three-pin anchor where the rappel goes down and climber’s right off a large overhang and hangs free, with the next station offset rather than straight below.
wa_south_face_5.descent_text: Standard descent rappels the upper West Ridge to a notch, then continues down the South Face to the glacier rather than reversing the Great Gash. From the summit, downclimb/scramble a few hundred feet toward a notch on the ridge, then begin rappelling. Multiple trip reports of this exact route confirm it as a sustained multi-rappel descent through a gully/notch system with no bolts; the stations are fixed pins, nuts and cord of variable quality, slung horns, or anchors built from gear (nuts, small-to-medium cams), so carry a rack sufficient for both the climb and for leaving/building rappel anchors, plus some cord or rap tat. One detailed trip report of this route logged 7 double-rope rappels, about three and a half down the West Ridge and four down the South Face, back to the Terror Glacier, building a fresh natural anchor at each station; a separate party descending the same general line but counting differently (single 70m rope, more, shorter pitches) reported roughly 5 rappels down the upper West Ridge to a notch followed by about 9 more rappels down through the gully/South Face terrain to the glacier, with several rappels traversing hard to one side to reach the next station and the final rappel using nearly the full rope length to reach a flat spot on the ice. Two ropes give the fewest rappels. The two-rope stations sit roughly 60 m apart and a single 70 m rope doubled reaches only about 35 m, so on one rope expect roughly twice as many stations: about 14 rappels of 30-35 m, which is what the single-rope party above ended up doing. Expect loose rock in the gully and real risk of the rope hanging up on the traversing raps, so back up rappels and check pulls carefully. The descent ends back on the Terror Glacier at the base of the West Ridge/South Face, from which you re-cross the icefall (same crevasse hazard as the approach, now on tired legs and possibly softer afternoon snow) to regain camp, then reverse the Terror Basin boot path and Goodell Creek Trail to the trailhead.

rappel_detail.notes: Made on the ascent, not the descent: a rappel of 100+ ft into the adjacent Zipper couloir. Two ropes recommended; a 70 m rope allows some downclimbing on moderate snow first.
rappel_detail.anchor: not described; bring slings
rappel_detail.station: The ridge top between Lover's Lane and the Zipper couloir, reached on the way up.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel from the tree unless the snow is good enough to downclimb, then plunge-step toward the Lane-Denman saddle and descend the steep gully on its far left side.
rappel_detail.anchor: a large tree a few feet below the summit
rappel_detail.station: Just below the summit, on the descent.

wa_lane_peak_r3.rappels: One roughly 100+ ft rappel (double rope recommended) from the ridge top into the adjacent Zipper couloir, made on the way up; on the descent, a rappel from a tree just below the summit is used unless the snow allows downclimbing
wa_lane_peak_r3.rappel_count_note: Two rappels in all: one of 100+ ft into the Zipper couloir on the way up, and one from a tree just below the summit on the way down, which good snow lets parties skip.
wa_lane_peak_r3.descent_text: From the summit, downclimb to a large tree a few feet below it and rappel from the tree unless the snow is good enough to downclimb. Then plunge-step down moderate slopes toward the Lane–Denman saddle; at the saddle, go to its far left side and descend a steep gully, then retrace the approach. The 100+ ft rappel from the ridge top into the adjacent Zipper couloir (double rope recommended; a 70m rope allows some downclimbing on moderate snow first) is part of the ascent, not the descent.

wa_live_free_or_die.rappel_count_note: This route finishes on Liberty Bell and takes the standard descent. Three rappels on a single 60 m rope, which is the rope this route recommends and the configuration these three stations describe. The count of two comes from the same station set rather than a different one: the first rappel, off the trees, is optional and replaces a downclimb of the ridge and the 5.6 boulder problem, so a party that downclimbs that section starts at the second station and reaches the ground in two single-rope rappels. Accounts recording two and accounts recording three are describing the same anchors. The two lower rappels are reported at about 25 m each, and a single 60 m rope reaches the first ledge with room to spare. This is the standard descent line shared with the East Face and Northwest Face routes. Parties who stop at M&M Ledge can instead descend Thin Red Line’s two-rope line: one rappel off the ledge and four more off bolts down the East Face.
wa_live_free_or_die.descent_text: Live Free or Die climbs the East Face for 8 pitches to M&M Ledge (roughly mid-height), then shares its final 3-4 pitches to the summit with the upper section of Thin Red Line. Parties who finish on the summit take the standard Liberty Bell descent. From the summit, downclimb the upper pitch a short way and go left (east) to a tree hung with rappel slings. One single-rope rappel with a 60 m rope reaches a sandy ledge; work right and down to a bolted station, then make two single-rope rappels of about 25 m from bolted anchors into the Liberty Bell-Concord notch at about 7,300 ft. Parties who downclimb the ridge and the 5.6 boulder problem to the first bolts instead of making the tree rappel do two rappels in all. From the notch, downclimb the loose gully back to the climbers’ path and the Blue Lake Trail. Parties who stop at M&M Ledge can instead take Thin Red Line’s rappel line: from M&M Ledge, rappel with two ropes off a fixed pin and wire, then work climber’s left to bolted anchors and make four more double-rope rappels to the talus at the base of the East Face.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 1 of 2, double-rope, to the notch between Middle and South Gunsight.
rappel_detail.anchor: south-facing rappel anchor near the summit
rappel_detail.station: Traverse south along the summit ridge from the top to the south-facing rappel anchors.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 2 of 2, double-rope, into the moat at the base of the notch.
rappel_detail.anchor: anchor at the Middle-South Gunsight notch
hazards: Loose, dirty and cold. Then navigate the crevasse field on the Chickamin Glacier back to camp.
rappel_detail.station: The notch between Middle and South Gunsight.

wa_east_face.rappels: 2 double-rope rappels: one from near the summit to the notch between Middle and South Gunsight, one more into the moat at the base of the notch. With only one 60 m rope expect roughly twice as many; no single-rope count is published.
wa_east_face.rappel_count_note: A first-hand report of the East Face 5.10d describes one double-rope rappel to the notch between Middle and South Gunsight, then one more — loose, dirty and cold — into the moat at the base of the notch. The figure of about four rappels on a single 60 m rope is arithmetic from roughly 100 m of descent rather than a published count.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 1 of 2, double-rope, to the notch between Middle and South Gunsight.
rappel_detail.anchor: south-facing rappel anchor near the summit
rappel_detail.station: Traverse south along the summit ridge from the top to the south-facing rappel anchors.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 2 of 2, double-rope, into the moat at the base of the notch.
rappel_detail.anchor: anchor at the Middle-South Gunsight notch
hazards: Loose, dirty and cold. Then navigate the crevasse field on the Chickamin Glacier back to camp.
rappel_detail.station: The notch between Middle and South Gunsight.

wa_sw_ridge.rappels: 2 double-rope rappels: one from near the summit to the notch between Middle and South Gunsight, one more into the moat at the base of the notch. With only one 60 m rope expect more; no single-rope count is published.
wa_sw_ridge.rappel_count_note: A first-hand report of the East Face 5.10d describes one double-rope rappel to the notch between Middle and South Gunsight, then one more — loose, dirty and cold — into the moat at the base of the notch. The figure of about four rappels on a single 60 m rope is arithmetic from roughly 100 m of descent rather than a published count.
wa_sw_ridge.descent_text: From the summit, traverse south along the summit ridge to the south-facing rappel anchors and make two double-rope rappels: the first to the notch between Middle and South Gunsight, the second into the moat at the base of the notch (loose, dirty and cold). With a single 60 m rope expect more rappels. From the glacier, reverse the approach: descend roughly 5,000 ft back to Agnes Creek and hike out 9-10 miles to High Bridge.

rappel_detail.pull: A rope end has jammed in a crack on the right side of this rappel, forcing the party to climb back up the other strand to free it - and the ground you would climb to reach it is loose. Watch where the ends land and pull away from the crack.
rappel_detail.notes: First rappel off the shared summit down to the P7 anchor on Mile High Club's line; single 60m rope reaches comfortably.
rappel_detail.anchor: summit rap rings, station ~8ft south of summit bolts and ~4ft off the ground
hazards: The edge below this station has cut a rope badly enough that the party had to chop it in half and retire it. The route page says the edge has since been ground down; the Beyond Redlining page still tells you exactly where to lay the rope, so treat it as live

A hard pendulum. The first-ascent advice is to lower to the large flake and walk left to the belay rather than rappelling free; a 2025 party swung hard right into a separate rock face on this rappel, on both of their visits
The nuts on these rap rings have been found loose - check them before you weight the station

Rappelling Beyond Redlining's own line is what this station exists to avoid: its first pitch is over 50 m, several pitches angle substantially left or right, and it needs angling rappels off single bolts, many of which only reach the next anchor on rope stretch
rappel_detail.station: Not on Beyond Redlining. From the shared summit, walk about 50 ft over to Mile High Club's top station: the rap rings sit back from the route's top, and the place to lay the rope is the least sharp part of the edge roughly 8 ft south of the bolts and about 4 ft off the ground. Toss just left of the crest, then angle down toward the lower anchor sitting at the foot of pitch 7. From here the whole descent stays about 10-15 ft skier's left of the bolt line, and for most pitches you can see the climbing anchors from the rap anchors.

rappel_detail.notes: A face-descent rappel down to the P6 anchor.
rappel_detail.anchor: P7 bolted/fixed station
hazards: Dropping to the dihedral-top anchor instead is a specific, named mistake - the station you want is above and left of it
The published reason for tossing left is that parties climb directly below: keep the rope and anything you knock loose off them
rappel_detail.station: Toss the rope slightly left of the bolt line rather than straight down. Rappel the pitch-6 face, then move to a rap anchor about 10 ft skier's left and 10 ft higher than the anchor atop the dihedral pitch. Do not continue to the top of the dihedral pitch.

rappel_detail.notes: A short rappel down to a ledge at P5; source explicitly flags this one as short.
rappel_detail.anchor: P6 station
hazards: Free-hanging above a ledge, so you arrive spinning onto a stance rather than sliding onto it
rappel_detail.station: A short rappel from the pitch-5 station to an anchor on a ledge off to the side of the dihedral pitch. It is free-hanging above the ledge.

rappel_detail.notes: Drops to P4, where one of two available anchor options is used.
rappel_detail.anchor: P5 ledge anchor
hazards: Most stations on this route have two anchors a few feet apart so ascending and descending parties do not share one - taking the wrong one puts you on top of climbers
Rope thrown from here lands on anyone on pitch 4 below
rappel_detail.station: Two anchors are available here; take the skier's-left one where you can, which keeps you off the climbing line.

rappel_detail.pull: A rope has been stuck in a crack pulling from the pitch-3 rap anchors; pull away from the crack. Feed the rope through the cedar bushes rather than throwing it.
rappel_detail.notes: The most commonly botched rappel on the descent — aim for a 10-ft-tall tree roughly 15 ft skier's-left of the climbing line; a hidden intermediate anchor is tucked in cedar bushes just below the visible upper-P3 station.
rappel_detail.anchor: P4 anchor
hazards: The route page states it outright: do not rappel down the vertical face on a single rope, because you will not reach the next anchors. Parties who miss it end up either doing two double-rope rappels from the top of pitch 3 or, on an 80 m, nearly reaching the pitch-2 anchors and then having to scramble across exposed ground
One party that missed it could not retrieve their rope at all - the pull angle around the intervening features made it stick and recovering it was judged unsafe
The tree the beta says will be flagged has never been flagged; years later the beta still only promises that it will be flagged soon
rappel_detail.station: The confusing one, and by a wide margin the most-reported problem on this descent. From the pitch-4 anchor, pass through cedar bushes directly below the station and rappel the low-angle upper part of pitch 3 - it is mostly walking. Aim for a tree about 10 ft tall standing roughly 15 ft skier's left of the climbing line; the intermediate anchor is tucked into a nook just below that tree. Look for it right where the ground turns from slabby to vertical. You cannot see this anchor on the way up, so it cannot be scouted on the climb; parties have found chalk arrows pointing at it.

rappel_detail.notes: Continues down to a lower-P3 anchor, landing on a large ledge.
rappel_detail.anchor: upper-P3 station (cedar-bush anchor)
hazards: This is the vertical face the station above exists to get you onto safely; it is the ground you would be stranded above having missed the nook
rappel_detail.station: From the nook anchor, rappel the vertical section at the start of pitch 3 down to a large ledge, and set up at one of the anchors on top of pitch 2 - the skier's-left one if it is free.

rappel_detail.notes: Drops to the P2 anchor.
rappel_detail.anchor: lower-P3 ledge anchor
hazards: Parties consistently record being surprised that the last anchor before the ground is a separate one, offset from the climbing anchor
rappel_detail.station: The station is NOT the pitch-1 climbing anchor, which is what people expect and head for. The rap anchor is about 10 ft down and 10-15 ft skier's left of the pitch-1 belay anchor.

rappel_detail.pull: Consider staying on rappel, walking back across to the belay bolt where the route starts, and pulling the rope from there.
rappel_detail.notes: Final rappel(s) via the P2 and P1 anchors bring you to the base of the route.
rappel_detail.anchor: P2 anchor, finishing at P1
hazards: Do not treat the base of the route as the ground - the ledge you land on is exposed and hundreds of feet up
The gully to climber's right throws natural rockfall onto the start of the scramble; keep helmets on until you are clear of it, especially with parties above
rappel_detail.station: The last rappel reaches the base of the route. Expect the starting ledge to be quite exposed, several hundred feet off the ground.

wa_beyond_redlining.rappels: Not recommended to rappel directly (angled rappels off single bolts, rope-length issues); standard descent rappels Mile High Club instead with a single 60m rope.
wa_beyond_redlining.rappel_count_note: Eight rappels down Mile High Club's line on a single 60 m rope. That configuration is newer than the route: a dedicated rappel line was added alongside Mile High Club in August 2019 specifically so the descent could be done on a single 60, and the eight-station descent dates from then. Before that, parties used a single 70 m or two 60 m ropes, and counts from that era differ honestly - eight single-rope rappels on a 70, or seven - so an older count disagreeing with this table describes the pre-2019 descent, not an error. The line stays about 10-15 ft skier's left of the bolt line throughout, and you should prefer the skier's-left anchor wherever two exist, because most stations are doubled so that rappelling and climbing parties are not on the same anchor. Beyond Redlining is equipped for rappelling but its own line is explicitly not recommended: the first pitch is over 50 m, several pitches angle substantially left or right, and it requires angling rappels off single bolts where many rappels only reach the next anchor on rope stretch. Beyond Redlining's own hardware - a mid-pitch-1 bail station, a missing maillon on pitch 3 - belongs to that line and not to this one. No per-station rappel distances are known for the Mile High Club descent, and the rappel line does not follow the climbing line, so the pitch lengths are not a substitute; the figures given are nominal rather than measured.
wa_beyond_redlining.descent_text: Do not rappel Beyond Redlining itself — official route beta explicitly says it is equipped for emergency use but 'not recommended' as a descent line, since the angle and pitch lengths make it a poor rap line that would need two ropes or a 70m rope with awkward hangs. Instead, from the shared summit, descend via Mile High Club's dedicated rappel line, which works with a single 60m rope over 8 rappels: summit rap rings down through P7, P6 (face descent), a short rap on P5 to a ledge, P4 to one of two available anchors, then the tricky 'upper P3' rappel — this one is the most commonly botched: aim for a 10-ft-tall tree roughly 15 ft skier's-left of the climbing line, where a hidden intermediate P3 anchor is tucked in cedar bushes just below the station; missing it and rapping straight down the vertical face below can leave you well short of the next anchor on a single rope. Below that, a lower-P3 rap drops to a large ledge, then P2 and P1 anchors bring you to the base. The first rap station off the summit is set back roughly 8 ft south of the summit bolts and about 4 ft off the ground — easy to walk past if you're not looking for it. Saddlebag your rope on the way down to avoid dropping loose rock or gear on parties below; ledges on this face hold loose material. Because Beyond Redlining offers limited bail options low on the route, parties should carry a 70m rope if there's any real chance of needing to retreat mid-climb rather than topping out to the shared summit.

rappel_detail.notes: First of three single-rope rappels down the south side toward the notch. Plan on near the full reach of a doubled 60 m rope.
rappel_detail.anchor: fixed station near summit
hazards: committing to the wrong descent is the easy mistake here - the bolted West Face rappels start well away from this line
rappel_detail.station: This is the classic line, not the bolted West Face one, and the two leave the summit from different places. Scramble down south and west of the summit, then down and skier's left toward the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire; the first fixed station is on that side.

rappel_detail.notes: Second single-rope rappel continuing toward the notch/gully.
rappel_detail.anchor: fixed station

rappel_detail.notes: Third single-rope rappel reaching the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire.
rappel_detail.anchor: fixed station at notch/gully
hazards: the notch is often still snow-covered in summer - expect a wet or snowy stance and possibly a footwear change at the anchor
rappel_detail.station: This rappel lands in the notch and Southwest Couloir between North and South Early Winters Spire.

rappel_detail.pull: Described as a double-rope rappel; check the pull before the second climber commits, since there is no way back up to the anchor once you are hanging free.
rappel_detail.notes: Largely free-hanging double-rope rappel past a huge chockstone (~50 ft/15m of air). Plan on a typical double-rope pitch.
rappel_detail.anchor: fixed station above chockstone
hazards: free-hanging and spinning below the chockstone
the anchor is webbing around a natural feature rather than hardware - inspect it and replace or back it up
rappel_detail.station: Fixed slings on the large chockstone blocking the couloir. The rappel goes off and past the chockstone and is largely free-hanging, about 50 ft of air.

rappel_detail.notes: Final short (~30 ft) rappel, or downclimb/scramble alternative, reaching the base of the Southwest Gully.
rappel_detail.anchor: tree anchor
rappel_detail.station: Short rappel of about 30 ft off a tree at the bottom of the couloir; scrambling and downclimbing is the accepted alternative if the tree or its slings look poor.

wa_news_nw_corner.rappels: Two lines: the bolted West Face (six bolted stations), all single-rope on a 60 m rope that just barely reaches - a 70 m is the comfortable choice - or the classic line (3 single-rope raps to the notch, then a largely free-hanging double-rope rappel past the chockstone, then a short tree rap)
wa_news_nw_corner.rappel_count_note: Two established descents. The bolted West Face line is six bolted single-rope stations; a 60 m rope only just reaches and a 70 m is the comfortable choice. The classic line is three single-rope rappels to the notch, a free-hanging double-rope rappel past the chockstone, then a short tree rappel or a downclimb to the ground; the table below lists the classic line.
wa_news_nw_corner.descent_text:
Two established ways off the summit; both are widely used and either works, but they return you to different spots relative to a gear stash at the base.

Bolted West Face rappel line (most direct back to packs at the base of NW Corner/West Face): from the summit, downclimb/walk skier's-left to the top of a clean, purpose-bolted rappel line down the right side of the West Face. Six bolted (2-bolt) rappel stations in a nearly direct line bring you back down to essentially the same spot where you left your pack at the base of the route. Pulls are reported as clean and the line is efficient — regulars find it a breeze. A single 60m rope is just barely sufficient (one station, reportedly the 3rd rappel, is tight enough that you may need to reach down to clip your PAS/daisy to the anchor and feed rope through your device to reach it); a 70m rope removes that squeeze and is the more comfortable choice. No natural anchors needed on this line — it's fully bolted.

Classic notch/chockstone descent (South/Southwest Gully): downclimb and rappel the south side into the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire, then continue down the Southwest Gully (the South Early Winter Spire "Chockstone Route" descent). This runs three single-rope rappels from near the summit down to the notch/gully (which often holds snow even in summer), followed by one spectacular, largely free-hanging double-rope rappel down and past a huge chockstone (~50 ft of air), then a final short rappel (~30 ft, off a tree anchor) or downclimb/scramble to reach the base. Total is about 4-5 rappels on this line. Anchors are natural/fixed slings around the chockstone and trees rather than bolts — inspect webbing before trusting it. Summit-to-base time on this descent is typically around 1.5-2 hours. This option is the standard descent if you climbed a route on the south/southwest side, or as a backup if the West Face bolt line is congested or iced.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel east down the gully to the Pernod-Chablis notch.
rappel_detail.anchor: Fixed nuts on the summit ridge (only reliable fixed anchor on route)

rappel_detail.notes: Continues down steep slabs toward the neve/snowfield.
rappel_detail.anchor: Natural anchor on steep slabs, unspecified and described as unreliable

rappel_detail.notes: Final rappel reaching the neve/snowfield below; two 60m ropes are needed for these lower rappels.
rappel_detail.anchor: Natural anchor on steep slabs, unspecified and described as unreliable

wa_direct_west_face.rappels: Multiple rappels (2x 60m ropes) east down the gully to the Pernod/Chablis notch, then more raps down steep slabs to the neve below
wa_direct_west_face.rappel_count_note: Individual lengths aren't given in feet/meters and exact per-rap distances aren't documented, so no per-station length is shown.
wa_direct_west_face.descent_text: From the top of the Direct West Face, rappel east down the gully to the Pernod-Chablis notch (rappel 1), then make a couple more rappels down steep slabs to the neve/snowfield below (rappels 2 and 3) — three rappels total to get off the technical ground. Two 60m ropes are needed for these. The only fixed rappel anchor on the route is on the summit ridge, where nuts have been left in place; everything else, including the old aid bolts used to reach the summit block (one reported missing a hanger, another loose in its hole), should be treated as unreliable — back up or build natural gear anchors in cracks/horns where you can. From the neve, trend north around the base of Chianti Spire and climb back up to Burgundy Col (~7,770 ft), then descend the climbers' path down the scree gullies to the bench camp and boot path back to the highway pullout. Budget real time for this — the three raps only get you to the neve, after which there's a substantial re-ascent to the col before the walk-off begins.

rappel_detail.pull: If you intend to link this with the next rappel, the technique reported is to flick the rope over a horn so it hangs down the correct side; check the pull line before the last climber commits.
rappel_detail.anchor: Fixed slings around a horn or flake at the top of the last pitch, on the ridge crest. There is no anchor on the summit itself — parties who go to the top build a gear belay there and traverse back to the crest station.
hazards: It is a ridge rappel rather than a face rappel: the start is awkward and the ropes want to run down either side of the crest
Loose rock is present throughout this descent and parties specifically credit helmets — keep the group off the fall line
rappel_detail.station: Reached by reversing the exposed summit slab traverse from the summit block back to the top of the final pitch. It is on the crest, not on a face.

rappel_detail.anchor: Fixed slings around a horn/flake at the foot of the crux (5.4-5.6) pitch.
hazards: If you take the linked option the rope only just reaches, and you arrive off-anchor — send the strongest scrambler first so they can get off rappel, reach the pitch-3 anchor and back up everyone behind
A rope that only just reaches is a rope that will not reach if the last person weights it lower or the ends are uneven; knot the ends
rappel_detail.station: At the base of the crux pitch, on the ascent line. It can be bypassed entirely: flicking the rope over a horn from station 1 lets a single 60 m rope doubled just reach the gully around the corner from the start of pitch 3, running rappels 1 and 2 as one roughly 30 m rappel.

rappel_detail.notes: Some parties shorten their ascent pitches deliberately so that they belay at these stations and know exactly where they are on the way down.
rappel_detail.anchor: Fixed slings around a horn or flake. At least one station on this descent was reported as a solid load-bearing horn with a useless backup beside it — a wad of slings looped around a handful of small loose rocks. Clip the horn; treat the wad as decoration.
hazards: Route-finding: this rappel does not follow the climbing line, so what you see on the way down is not what you climbed
Loose rock on and below the station
rappel_detail.station: Below a long scrambling section that separates rappels 2 and 3, and it is one of the hard ones to find. Parties consistently report that the stations here are not obvious and recommend spotting and remembering them on the way up. This rappel also wanders off the ascent line.

rappel_detail.pull: A long rappel on joined ropes over broken ridge terrain: set the knot deliberately and confirm the pull before the last climber leaves the station.
rappel_detail.notes: Some parties skip the final downclimb and instead rappel the loose gully straight from the notch. From the notch it is scree, talus and boot path back into the basin.
rappel_detail.anchor: Sling anchor near the west notch below the technical climbing.
hazards: Easy to overshoot or drift onto the wrong side of the crest — one party ended up on the north side of the ridge and had to solo an exposed, loose pitch of 4th class to regain it
The gully below the notch is dirty and loose whether you rappel it or downclimb it
rappel_detail.station: The last and longest rappel, returning to the west notch. It wants two ropes joined, or a 60 m doubled if you can find a station that puts it in reach.

wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.rappels: Descend the West Ridge rap line: about 4 rappels, two single-rope rappels, a scramble, another single, then a longer double-rope rappel to the west notch; parties heading for the South Gully often take only the first two and downclimb
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.rappel_count_note: Commonly described as four stations (two singles, one single, one double-rope rappel); some trip reports collapse this to three depending on how stations are combined.
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.descent_text: Most parties do not reverse the East Ridge; the accepted descent is to finish near the summit, traverse to the top of the West Ridge, and go down using the West Ridge's established rappel line (two single-rope rappels past the crux, a short scramble, another single, then a double-rope rappel to the west notch - see the West Ridge descent for full detail) before dropping back to the basin and Ingalls Creek. Some parties do reverse the East Ridge directly, especially when combining the climb with the nearby Balanced Rock feature: this involves downclimbing/rappelling a vertical chimney using chained-together fixed rappel slings, then a rappel down a steep gully to an exposed slab, then another rappel after crossing the slab, finishing with class 3 downclimbing to the 8,000-ft notch. Expect roughly 2-4 short single-rope rappels off existing (sometimes weathered) fixed slings and chains rather than full ropelength raps; a 50m rope was reported as sufficient. Back up any suspect fixed anchors with your own gear. From the notch/basin, reverse the approach: descend to Ingalls Creek Trail, cross the creek, and climb back over Longs Pass to the trailhead.

wa_sherpa_peak_west_ridge.rappels: About four rappels down the ascent line: three single-rope rappels (with a scramble between the second and third), then a final, longer double-rope rappel to the west notch. Parties combine or split stations differently, so expect 3-5.
wa_sherpa_peak_west_ridge.rappel_count_note: Commonly described as four stations (two singles, one single, one double-rope rappel); some trip reports collapse this to three depending on how stations are combined.
wa_sherpa_peak_west_ridge.descent_text: The standard descent reverses the West Ridge using a sequence of rappels rather than downclimbing the whole route. From the summit area, two single-rope rappels lead down past the crux (5.4-5.6) pitch to a short 3rd-class scramble; this is followed by another single-rope rappel and then a longer double-rope rappel (two ropes joined, or a single 60m doubled) that returns you to the west notch below the technical climbing. Anchors are a mix of fixed slings around horns and flakes; most are solid (slings around big, well-set flakes/horns), but at least one reported station was backed by a sketchy bundle of slings wrapped around a few small loose rocks next to the actual load-bearing horn - inspect and back up questionable tat with your own gear. Some parties skip the last downclimb and instead rappel directly down the loose, dirty gully from the notch. Bring a 60m rope (or two ropes for the double-rope stretch) and extra slings/cord to replace weathered anchors. From the notch, descend scree/talus and boot path back into the basin (glissading is possible on lingering snow) to camp, then reverse the approach over Longs Pass to the trailhead. Total rappel count is commonly described as four stations (two singles, a scramble, one more single, then one double-rope rappel); some parties count this as three rappels depending on how stations are combined, so expect 3-4 total.
